title: Decodable Books vs. Leveled Readers: The View from the Reading League
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood, a former reading clinician, uses excerpts from a Reading League chapter video to lay out the competing assumptions behind leveled readers and decodable books. Leveled books are written to carry meaning at graded linguistic complexity so a reader works at the edge of their ability, while decodables treat meaning as largely irrelevant and focus attention on letters and phonemes. The science-of-reading view sees leveled books as inviting guessing and lacking control over phonics scope and sequence. Underwood locates the root of the Reading Wars in that view's claim that phonics is the only instruction with scientific evidence, and he notes decodables have their own problem of being nonsensical. He warns of legislation requiring decodables exclusively and argues the real question is how to begin reading instruction so that children learn both skills and strategies.
points: Leveled readers and decodables are built for different purposes: graded meaningful language for scaffolded practice versus controlled letter-sound patterns for explicit teaching.
The science-of-reading critique is that leveled books invite predicting and picture clues that encourage guessing over sounding out.
The crux of the Reading Wars is the assumption that phonics is the only scientifically supported instruction and must be mastered before other behaviours.
Decodables are hard to write and often nonsensical, so neither type is free of trade-offs.
Underwood objects to legislating decodables exclusively and says the argument is about how best to begin instruction so readers develop skills and habits of mind.
quotes: Leveled books are written to express a meaningful story or explain an idea just as any other book but with measured levels of linguistic complexity to reduce demands on interacting psycholinguistic processes. The idea is to have a continuum from less to more complex language in order to accommodate a reader-text match at an independent, instructional, and frustration level.

Decodable books are designed for a different purpose with a completely different focus during the writing process. The meaning of the written text is largely irrelevant. Instead, these books are designed under the assumption that calling attention to the meaning of a word is an instructional distraction. High frequency words—words that take up most of the syntactic slots in language structures—are a necessary evil and are kept to a minimum.

The SoR operates under the assumption that phonics instruction is the only type of reading instruction supported with scientific evidence while other instructional approaches are ill-informed or misguided. “You can’t decode words if you don’t know short vowels, and you can’t read if you can’t decode.

Writing decodable books is not easy. Leveled books with their concern for subject matter are fun to write and even read but make it hard to drill down on short vowels, the gulf between pre-decoding and decoding.

The proposition that regular classroom teachers ought to be required by legislation to reject leveled readers and use decodable books exclusively until readers achieve mastery of basic phonics is gaining support. The Reading League has built a state by state slate of chapters working to establish this SoR view of reading instruction regardless of widespread criticism of its narrow, almost atheoretical perspective.

Leveled books are designed to afford expert reading practice with a variety of cognitive processes operating simultaneously to produce comprehension at the cusp of a reader’s psycholinguistic capacity. Reading is, after all, a language process, not a perceptual process. Side-of-the-pool instruction is needed as appropriate, but guided practice in the face of as much complexity as a reader can handle productively is the engine of growth.
